1.point: Draw the reader in through a familiar Ramadan experience and announce that the chapter sets out emptying, its five disciplines and how much of each to take.
steps: A hook: the Munajat line and the fact that readers already keep these disciplines in Ramadan without naming them.
A one-breath recall of the four stages, then the announcement of what the chapter will do.

2.point: Proper irfan starts at the second stage, emptying the heart, and the five disciplines are the tools of that stage.
steps: Polishing is the first stage and any believer's work; irfan proper begins at the next stage, which Ibn Sina names as emptying.
Emptying means clearing the heart of whatever occupies it other than God, and this is harder than keeping the law.
Clearing does not mean loving nothing else; what goes is what diverts the heart.
Emptying has an internal structure (Ibn Sina's four steps) that the later sections map the disciplines onto.
The five disciplines target the heart, so they are the tools of emptying rather than of polishing.
Conclusion: emptying is the second stage and the five are its tools.

3.point: Silence, hunger and the night prayer each close an opening (tongue, stomach, sleep) through which the world crowds the heart.
steps: Silence closes the tongue, and what silence means.
Hunger closes the stomach, and what hunger means.
How the two work on the heart: they block the chain of idle thoughts.
The night prayer closes sleep, with the Qur'an's command and its stated reason: the night frees attention.
All three work the same way, by freeing the heart's attention for God.

4.point: Seclusion is Ibn Sina's first step (separating the heart from distraction) and remembrance is his second (dusting off the traces that separation leaves).
steps: Shia seclusion is seclusion of the heart, not of the body, and it maps onto Ibn Sina's first step.
The Qur'an asks for this seclusion (tabattul), and the Prophet's life among people shows it is of the heart.
Separation leaves traces; remembrance dusts them off, as Ibn Sina's second step, with a present effect in the heart.
The effect is present because remembrance is answered by God's favour.
Conclusion: seclusion separates, remembrance dusts off.

5.point: No discipline is taken in full; each is dosed to what the person can carry, started small and kept up.
steps: None of the five is kept to the full; even the Qur'an eased the night prayer.
The measure is what the person can carry, not imitation of the Prophet.
Concretely: start small, grow only with eagerness, keep one practice for at least a year.
The same measures apply to the remaining disciplines (hunger, wakefulness, remembrance, seclusion).
Conclusion: a small, sustained dose measured to the person.

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: The hook: ties the Munajat line and the reader's own Ramadan to the disciplines before they are named.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Recalls the four stages in two sentences and states what the chapter will establish; this is the announcement the opening exists for.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Step 1: polishing is the first stage; irfan proper begins at emptying, on Ibn Sina's authority.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Step 2: defines emptying as clearing the heart of what occupies it other than God and shows why it is harder than the law; the salah example is in-paragraph support.

¶5.label: support
¶5.why: Guards the definition in ¶4 against the misreading that emptying means loving nothing; Section 4's seclusion-of-the-heart argument (¶17, ¶19) relies on this distinction.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: Supplies Ibn Sina's four steps, which ¶17, ¶21 and ¶31 all depend on. The non-swimmer image and the sentence on the self are more than the step needs, but the paragraph is load-bearing.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Names the five disciplines and gives the reason they belong to emptying (their target is the heart). The two Lantern of the Path quotations on rest and wakefulness are not used by anything and could go.

¶8.label: restate
¶8.why: Repeats the conclusion already supplied by ¶3 and ¶7; the three-doors/two-on-the-heart split is a signpost, not a step.

¶9.label: advance
¶9.why: First door: silence and what it means. The Tabatabaʾi/Imam al-Rida citation only supports the definition.

¶10.label: advance
¶10.why: Second door: hunger and what it means, with the mechanism (a full stomach draws the soul's attention). The ʿUnwan al-Basri counsel is in-paragraph support.

¶11.label: advance
¶11.why: Supplies the common mechanism for the first two doors: they block the chain of idle thoughts that fills the heart. The second half (muraqaba, the ascension hadith) is a second source on silence and wisdom that nothing later uses.

¶12.label: advance
¶12.why: Third door: sleep, and the Qur'anic basis for the night prayer.

¶13.label: support
¶13.why: A one-sentence bridge that frames the verse ¶14 explains; the 'half the night' detail is reused in ¶25.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: The reason the night frees attention, which is the step that makes sleep a 'door'. The sentence on showing seriousness and the Prophet as example is extra; al-Dhariyat is a second witness.

¶15.label: advance
¶15.why: The unifying step: all three disciplines free the heart's attention. This is the section's real conclusion.

¶16.label: restate
¶16.why: States the conclusion a second time immediately after ¶15 and adds only a transition.

¶17.label: advance
¶17.why: Step 1 of the section: Shia seclusion is of the heart, mapped onto Ibn Sina's first step. The Sufi forty-days comparison is context the argument does not use.

¶18.label: support
¶18.why: One-sentence bridge introducing the verse that ¶19 interprets.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: Reads the verse through the Prophet's life to show that the seclusion asked for is of the heart; the cave image makes the step land.

¶20.label: support
¶20.why: Gives the practical form seclusion takes (the night prayer); borderline, since the point concerns function, and ¶29 says the same thing again.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Step: remembrance dusts off the traces separation leaves, as Ibn Sina's second step, with a present effect; sets up ¶23.

¶22.label: aside
¶22.why: Identifies 'frequent' with the Tasbih of al-Zahraʾ and adds the Sufi/Shia contrast on who assigns the words. Nothing later depends on it; the minimum-dose material belongs to Section 5 and the assignment contrast is unused.

¶23.label: support
¶23.why: Explains why the effect claimed in ¶21 is present: remembrance is answered by God's favour.

¶24.label: restate
¶24.why: Repeats the section's point, which ¶17 and ¶21 already stated, and re-lists the five.

¶25.label: advance
¶25.why: Step 1: none of the five is kept in full; the Qur'an itself eased the night prayer.

¶26.label: advance
¶26.why: Step 2: the measure is what the person can carry, not imitation of the Prophet.

¶27.label: advance
¶27.why: Step 3: small at first, grown only with eagerness, kept up for a year; this is where 'small and kept up' is supplied.

¶28.label: support
¶28.why: Extends the measure to hunger, wakefulness and remembrance from the written guides, which the point's 'each discipline' needs; but it opens as corroboration ('the same measures') and three sources repeat one idea. The medicine line that titles the section could sit in ¶26.

¶29.label: support
¶29.why: Extends the measure to seclusion and gives its upper bound (forty-day austerities not desirable). The Kernel room and the Lantern line on every prophet are corroboration, and the nightly hour repeats ¶20.

¶30.label: restate
¶30.why: A full summary of Sections 2 to 5; every sentence was stated before.

¶31.label: restate
¶31.why: Repeats ¶6 (the self goes last) and ¶2 (the last stages are God's work), then closes on a question the chapter does not answer.
